title: Historic Baddow House with resident ghost seeks new owner for $3m
byline: Samantha Healy, Property Journalist First published 15 Sep 2026, 2:26pm
excerpt: It was once a ghost tour destination. Now this heritage mansion rumoured to be haunted by a heartbroken ghost has been listed for sale following a multimillion dollar renovation.
content:
Baddow House at 366 Queen St, Maryborough, is for sale

It is rumoured to be one of the most haunted houses in Australia, and was once a ghost tour destination for those who hoped to hear things go bump in the night.

Now this significant heritage home is ready for its next chapter.

The iconic house

Current owner Martin Simons, a journalist, purchased heritage-listed Baddow House in Maryborough, considered one of the nation’s most haunted towns, in 2016 from author Anne de Lisle and her husband Ian Russell after they completed a $2 million-plus renovation.

That renovation journey was turned into a book called A Grand Passion.

“The government bought it after the war and were going to turn it into a returned veterans home,” Mr Simons said.

“But it was never used for that and sat vacant for about 10 years and vagrants moved in.

“It is supposed to be one of the most haunted houses in Queensland but I have never felt any supernatural occurrences.

“However, we have had open house events and some people say they feel strange but I think it depends on your frame of mind.”

Baddow House was built in 1883

Baddow House was built in 1883 for prominent settler Edgar Aldridge and his family.

Aldridge established hotels, stores and wharves in Maryborough.

“The first years of settlement were extraordinarily troubled with deadly conflict between Europeans and Aborigines,” the Queensland Heritage Register says.

“This situation discouraged settlement. Aldridge petitioned the New South Wales government to send extra troopers in order to encourage settlement.”

Edgar and Maria Aldridge

Aldridge died in 1888 and the house passed onto his son Harry until his death in 1910.

Two years later, the Bank of NSW foreclosed on the property and sold it at auction.

Baddow House then passed through many hands.

Folklore has it that the mansion is haunted by Esse Eldridge, the daughter of Harry, who was supposedly so devastated after her family lost the house to foreclosure that she wiped her tears on the walls and continues to linger around the mansions grand cedar staircase.

It was then believed to have been used as a boarding house for the local Catholic school before it was transferred to the Crown, which, according to the Heritage Register, intended to use it as a migrant hostel.

But it remained empty and was badly vandalised.

The formal dining room

It was then used as a meeting hall by the Boy Scouts and then parts of the estate were sold off, with the remainder held by the Crown to preserve the Old Maryborough Town Site.

The grand formal lounge

Passing through more hands, Baddow House at various times operated as a museum, wedding and events venue, and ghost tour destination, but is now a private residence.

Mr Simons said Baddow House has had 16 owners during its lifetime.

“It could be a grand home or a business,” he said.

Baddow House has five bedrooms, three bathrooms and sits on a 7284sq m block.

One of the bathrooms

It is listed with Queensland Sotheby’s International Realty agent Lynn Malone for offers around $3 million.

The Georgian-style manor boasts 5m-high ceilings, multiple formal and informal living rooms, six fireplaces, wide verandahs, cypress ash and hoop pine floors, solid red cedar ceiling-to-floor interior doors, drawing rooms, a country kitchen, a library, an office, and a separate garden studio.

The country kitchen

It is neighboured by 74 acres of Crown heritage-listed parklands containing the original town site.

Ms Malone said Baddow House offered “an irreplaceable combination of legacy and lifestyle as a family home, with future income potential, operating as a tourism/wedding venue and at a purchase price that is unfathomable compared with Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide and Canberra”.

“It is regarded as the Fraser Coast’s most significant 19th-century residence,” she said.

“Baddow House is recognised as one of Queensland’s most important heritage-listed residences and celebrated as an authentic heritage home with historic dynasty provenance and commercial potential.”

One of the bedrooms

Mr Simons said it was a reluctant sale but he had been convinced by loved ones that it was time to downsize.

“You have to move on,” he said.

Unless you are Esse Eldridge, perhaps?
